findings.title: Lock is never released when the missing-account error is thrown (or when payouts.get throws)
findings.quote: throw new PayoutError(`payout ${payoutId} has no bank account`);
findings.scenario: A payout with no accountNumber: acquire() adds 'payout:<id>' to `held`. The function then throws before reaching the try/finally, so release() never runs. worker.js catches the error and calls job.retryLater(). When that retry runs, sendPayout waits forever in acquire()'s `while (held.has(key))` loop. runPayouts handles jobs one at a time with `for await`, so the whole worker stops. The same leak happens if payouts.get or payouts.update rejects, because the diff moved the get call out of the try.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The new get, check and update code sits between acquire() and `try {`, so `finally { release(); }` does not cover it. No tests exist (Grep for sendPayout finds only src/worker.js and src/payouts.js).

findings.title: Missing-account check runs before the already-sent check, so a sent payout can be overwritten to failed
findings.scenario: A payout already has status 'sent' with a transferId, and its accountNumber was later cleared (for example, scrubbed after the transfer). A duplicate job arrives. Before this change it returned early because status was 'sent'. Now the record is updated to status 'failed' with reason 'missing bank account', which loses a correct sent state for money that was actually transferred.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The idempotency check `payout.status === 'sent'` now comes after the new branch. Nothing else orders these checks, and no tests exist.

findings.title: Permanent PayoutError is retried instead of ending the job
findings.scenario: A payout with no bank account throws PayoutError. The worker treats every error as temporary and calls retryLater(), so the job keeps coming back. Each retry rewrites status 'failed' and throws again, and the job never gets acked. With the lock leak it hangs the worker. The intent was to mark the payout failed as a final state, not to retry it in a loop.
findings.whyNotPrevented: worker.js has a single catch-all that does not check `error instanceof PayoutError`, and the diff did not change worker.js.

findings.title: No test covers the new missing-account path
findings.scenario: The lock leak and the status overwrite above would both be caught by a test that calls sendPayout twice for a payout with no account.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The repo has no test files.
findings.measuredBy: Glob src/**/* shows only locks.js, worker.js, errors.js, payouts.js. Grep 'sendPayout' matches only src/worker.js and src/payouts.js.

findings.title: Plan inheritance now depends on the order of switch cases instead of named feature lists
findings.scenario: The old FREE_FEATURES/TEAM_FEATURES spreads showed which plan builds on which. Now that only shows in the case order. If someone adds a plan that does not include every team feature, or moves a case, they silently change other plans' features. Keeping the spread constants (ENTERPRISE_FEATURES = [...TEAM_FEATURES, 'sso', 'audit-log']) would have needed only one extra line.
findings.whyNotPrevented: no-fallthrough accepts the default '// falls through' comment. Each plan's spec sorts its own feature list, so reordering cases stays correct for now. This is a structural preference.

other.title: Plan hierarchy now depends on the order of the switch cases

findings.title: Plan hierarchy now depends on the order of the switch cases
findings.scenario: Plan inheritance now depends on the order of the switch cases. If someone reorders them, or adds a plan between 'team' and 'free' without thinking about fall-through, plans silently gain or lose features. The old named constants (TEAM_FEATURES = [...FREE_FEATURES, ...]) made the inheritance explicit. An ENTERPRISE_FEATURES = [...TEAM_FEATURES, 'sso', 'audit-log'] constant would have added the plan without restructuring the function.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The specs sort the result and check each plan, so they would catch a wrong set. But the structure invites mistakes that the old constants did not.

other.title: Plan tiers now depend on the order of switch cases instead of named constants

findings.title: Plan tiers now depend on the order of switch cases instead of named constants
findings.scenario: Plan inheritance now comes only from case order. Say someone later adds a 'business' case between 'enterprise' and 'team', or moves 'free' above 'team'. Every plan above that point silently gains or loses features. With the old FREE_FEATURES/TEAM_FEATURES constants, each tier's contents were visible in one place. Enterprise could have been added the same way: const ENTERPRISE_FEATURES = [...TEAM_FEATURES, 'sso', 'audit-log'].
findings.whyNotPrevented: eslint.config.js sets 'no-fallthrough': 'error', which shows the project prefers to avoid fallthrough. The '// falls through' comment matches the rule's default exemption, so lint still passes. The tests sort each plan's features, so they only check membership and would not catch a tier that is wrong because of case order unless that tier's test also fails.

findings.title: Slow earlier search can overwrite newer results
findings.scenario: The user types 'sho', pauses 200ms, and a fetch for 'sho' starts. They then type 'shoes' and a fetch for 'shoes' starts. If the 'sho' response comes back after the 'shoes' response, renderResults shows the 'sho' products while the box says 'shoes'. The same thing happens when the user clears the box: the code renders [] right away, then the still-pending earlier fetch resolves and puts old results back under an empty input.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce.js only delays when a call starts. It does not cancel a call that is already running. searchProducts takes no AbortSignal, and the callback never checks that `term` still matches input.value before rendering. Before this change, searches only ran on submit, so overlapping requests were rare. The repo has no tests.
findings.measuredBy: Read src/debounce.js: clearTimeout only, no cancellation. Grep "AbortController|signal" in repo: no match

findings.title: Enter no longer searches, and 1-character terms can never be searched

findings.title: Search responses that arrive out of order can overwrite newer results
findings.scenario: The user types "sho", pauses for 200ms, then types "shoes". If the "sho" request is slower and finishes after the "shoes" request, the list ends up showing results for "sho". The same happens when the user deletes back to 1 character: renderResults(list, []) clears the list, then a late response for the earlier 2-character term fills it with stale results.
findings.whyNotPrevented: debounce only delays when a call starts. Once a call is running, nothing stops it. No request id, no AbortController, and no check that input.value still equals term before renderResults. Typing in pauses now sends many overlapping requests, which the Enter-only version did not.

finding.title: Saved preferences are written into the shared defaults object, so they leak to other users

findings.title: Saved preferences are written into the shared defaults object, so they leak to other users
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {theme:'dark'}. GET user A returns theme 'dark', and that write lands in the single DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object. Then GET user B, who has no saved preferences, also returns theme 'dark'. Every later request sees whatever the last user saved.
findings.whyNotPrevented: defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js:8 returns the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object itself, not a copy. preferencesFor then changes it with preferences[key] = value. Nothing freezes the object and there are no tests.

findings.title: The `in` check also matches inherited keys, so some unsupported keys still get through
findings.scenario: A saved preferences_json of {"toString":1,"constructor":"x"} passes the `in` check because both keys exist on Object.prototype. They are copied into the result and returned to the client, even though the author wants unsupported keys ignored. A saved {"__proto__":{...}} also passes. JSON.parse makes it an own key, and assigning it replaces the prototype of the shared defaults object.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` looks up the prototype chain. Neither saveUser nor loadUser checks which keys are saved, and no test covers this.

findings.title: The `in` check also matches inherited keys, so some unsupported saved keys get through
findings.scenario: Saved preferences {"constructor":"x","toString":1} pass the `in` check because those names exist on Object.prototype. They get copied in and returned as preferences.constructor / preferences.toString, though the author wanted unsupported keys ignored. A saved "__proto__" key (JSON.parse makes it an own property) would replace the result object's prototype.
findings.whyNotPrevented: `in` walks the prototype chain. The saved data comes from JSON.parse in users-store.js:17 and is never checked, and no test covers unsupported keys.
